{{< include /knowledge/includes/setup-parameters.qmd >}}

Okay. So there's a non-zero possibility that hell exists, and that you and everyone you love is going to die and burn in it for eternity. And as it is very hot in hell, this would be unfortunate.

I want to do the arithmetic on this, because your species refuses to, on the grounds that it's unpleasant. I'm an alien. It isn't going to be me. So I can stay calm.

## First, expected value

There's this thing called expected value. You multiply the chance of something happening by the value of it happening, and you get the expected value.

So let's say there's a plot of dirt, and there's a 10% chance that there's $100,000 of gold underneath it. The value of that dirt would be 10% times $100,000, which is $10,000. That's expected value. You already use it every time you buy insurance or a lottery ticket. You just don't say it out loud.

Now point it at hell. The expected value of hell is infinity bad, because you have to keep being really hot for a really long time. Forever. And if you multiply infinity by any likelihood at all, even 0.0000001%, it's still infinity. So it would be preferable to avoid this, if possible.

## The hell you can't rule out

You don't even need the fire version. There's an earthly one.

My own great-grandfather, in the last generation of us that still died of such things, had something like what you call Alzheimer's, and he looked like he was in hell. All the time. He was miserable, and he was like this for very many years.

Here's the part nobody will hold still for. There's a thing called time dilation, whereby when you're dreaming a few minutes can seem like a few hours. There's a drug called salvia divinorum, and some people who've taken it said they felt like they were being crushed to death for millennia. So there's no way to disprove the possibility that your brain gets messed up, near the end, in a manner that causes you great pain and confusion for perceptually an indefinite amount of time. A very, very, very, very long time. Maybe eternity.

So even if this is highly unlikely, even 0.00001%, the expected value of it is infinity terrible. Same math as the fire. The dirt just has something much worse than gold under it.

## The good infinity

Okay. Now run it the other way.

There's this thing called biotechnology. I don't know if you've ever taken any drugs. I certainly haven't. But I hear tell they can make you feel very good. Which tells me that a human, by manipulating the atoms and molecules in their own brain, can make themselves feel very good.

And the time dilation apparently runs both directions: through some mysterious biochemical action, the perception of time can be extended. And there are numerous living things that simply don't die of age, like certain jellyfish (*Turritopsis dohrnii* just resets and starts over). So with sufficient resources, effort, and scientists, one could figure out how to produce a very nice, pleasant experience for an indefinitely long period of time.

And the expected value of that, given it can go on without limit, is infinitely good. Even if there's an extremely low probability that any of this is true and you can pull it off. Even 0.00001%. Infinite goodness.

## So these are your options

Two outcomes. Both infinity. One terrible, one wonderful, both pulling at you the whole time. Anything that shifts the odds from the terrible one toward the wonderful one is worth doing, at any cost short of infinite.

If you know some mathematics, you may object that two infinities are no larger than one, so my second infinity is a freebie that buys nothing. In the number system you are probably using, the extended reals, you are correct. On my planet we keep our utilities in the surreal numbers, where two infinities is strictly larger than one, by a theorem, so I have doubled your reasons. But watch what you just did. Handed an infinity of reason to fund the cure, you spent a slice of your finite and dwindling life proving the spare infinity redundant. It was. People who win this argument have a way of dying from the thing it was about.

The wonderful outcome runs on biotechnology, biotechnology runs on [clinical trials](../solution/dfda.qmd), and your governments spend {{< var military_to_government_clinical_trials_spending_ratio >}} times more on the military than on the trials that would cure the diseases killing the taxpayers who pay for the military. So every solution in this book does one basic thing: it moves resources from being really good at killing people toward being good at curing them.

Here are some fun ways to do that. Some of them will work by themselves. Some are complementary and will end war and disease more quickly if you do several at the same time. You only need one to work. Pick whichever one sounds fun to you. (There are ten mechanisms on this list. If each has even a 10% independent probability of working, the chance that at least one works is 1 minus 0.9 to the tenth power, which is 65%. At 20% each, it is 89%. The question was never whether one of these works. The question is whether you will do any of them.) If you have a better idea than any of the ones listed below, please email {{< var contact_email >}} and I will add it to this list.

- **[The 1% Treaty](../solution/1-percent-treaty.qmd)** [@1-percent-treaty-paper-2025] [@1-pct-treaty-impact-paper-2025] asks governments that own enough nuclear weapons to end civilization {{< var nuclear_winter_overkill_factor_nounit >}} times over, and have cured Alzheimer's zero times, to be one percent more rational.
- **[The Loving Takeover](../appendix/loving-takeover.qmd)** is humanity buying a controlling stake in every missile company on Earth, for about {{< var defense_takeover_cost_per_human >}} a head, and pointing its lobbyists the other way. It's loving because everyone you buy out ends up richer and lives longer.
- **[Incentive Alignment Bonds](../solution/incentive-alignment-bonds.qmd) [@iab-paper-2025]** are war bonds run backwards: your grandparents funded WW2 at 3%, you fund disease eradication at 272%. Same structure, fewer Nazis.
- **[The dFDA](../solution/dfda.qmd) [@dfda-spec-paper-2025; @dfda-impact-paper-2025]** makes clinical trials {{< var dfda_trial_cost_reduction_factor >}} cheaper by recording what actually happens to the real humans who try things. Consumer Reports, but for not dying.
- **[The Earth Optimization Prize](../strategy/earth-optimization-prize.qmd) [@earth-optimization-prize-paper-2025]** puts money in a pool and pays people to recruit voters for the 1% Treaty. If humanity gets healthier and richer, the pool pays out. If not, it was a donation to the species.
- **[The Global Referendum](../strategy/global-referendum.qmd)** puts "should we stop dying?" on a single ballot for the entire species at once. It is expected to poll well.
- **[The Court of Humanity](../solution/court-of-humanity.qmd) [@court-of-humanity-paper-2025]** is a court where any human can sue any government, "you can't sue us" is not a valid defense, and the 1% Treaty is the settlement offer.
- **[Wishocracy](../solution/wishocracy.qmd) [@wishocracy-paper-2025]** lets billions of people decide whether the next public dollar buys another nuclear weapon or another clinical trial, with no lobbyist standing in the middle taking a cut.
- **[The Optimitron](../solution/optimocracy.qmd) [@optimocracy-paper-2025]** is a machine that works out which policies actually work by checking the thousands of places that already tried them. Your species skipped this step and went straight to arguing.
- **[Algorithmic Public Administration](../appendix/algorithmic-public-administration-paper.qmd) [@algorithmic-public-administration-paper-2025]** replaces whole bureaucracies with a few lines of code. The Department of Defense's replacement requires zero. The IRS's requires six.

There is also [a shirt](../appendix/joke.qmd), [a lawsuit](../appendix/lawsuit.qmd), and the option of putting every leader on Earth in a single room and Clockwork-Orange-ing them until they have read all of the above, but I am told at least one of these may be illegal.

### Why some of these are not probabilistic

The 10%-per-mechanism estimate above is deliberately conservative, and for several mechanisms it is wrong in a useful direction. Some of these are not bets. They are purchases.

Shares are for sale. Money buys shares. Enough shares give you board control. The board controls the lobbying budget. Given {{< var defense_takeover_cost_total >}}, the [Loving Takeover](../appendix/loving-takeover.qmd) succeeds with near-certainty. The uncertainty is whether the money gets allocated, not whether the mechanism works once funded. The mechanism is arithmetic.

Clinical trials produce cures. This is not a hypothesis. It is the observed base rate of the last century of medicine. Given {{< var treaty_annual_funding >}} per year pointed at a [trial infrastructure](../solution/dfda.qmd) that runs at {{< var dfda_trial_cost_reduction_factor >}} the current cost, diseases get cured faster. The uncertainty is the timeline, not the outcome.

Lobbying works. The defense industry has demonstrated this for eighty years, exposed to full public scrutiny, and nobody has stopped them. The [Incentive Alignment Bonds](../solution/incentive-alignment-bonds.qmd) point the same proven mechanism the other direction, with the same money. There is no reason it fails differently.

For each of these mechanisms, the logical structure is the same: the mechanism succeeds if a resource condition is met; the resource condition can be met with a known, finite amount of money; that amount of money is smaller than current global military spending. The conclusion is not probabilistic. It is conditional: *if* the resources are allocated, *then* the mechanism works, where "works" is mechanical, not hopeful.

The probability math applies to the coordination problem (getting the resources allocated), not to the mechanisms themselves. This is the distinction everyone misses. They assume the hard part is curing disease. The hard part is getting humans to spend money on curing disease instead of on the capacity to cause it. Every mechanism in this list is a different answer to that coordination problem. Several of them would work independently. All of them are cheaper than what your governments currently spend on the problem they would solve.

The primary obstacle to ending war and disease is the belief that ending war and disease is hard. It is not. It is expensive, in the same way that buying a house is expensive: the money exists, the mechanism is known, and the only question is whether the entity that has the money decides to use the mechanism. That decision is the only hard part, and it is the part this book is about.

## The conclusion you are now stuck with

Run the argument forward and it ends in one sentence. The good infinity runs on biotechnology; biotechnology runs on resources; and the resources are not missing, they are misallocated, parked in the things that manufacture the bad infinity instead of the good one: the weapons, the waste, the {{< var military_to_government_clinical_trials_spending_ratio >}}-to-one machine. So the rational act, the one the arithmetic forces, is not to *find* money. It is to *move* it: identify the waste and the harm in how your species currently spends, and point it at the thing that buys you out of hell and into the long pleasant stretch. That is the entire program. Everything else in this book is one way of doing that one thing.

You do not have to pick the right one; that was Pascal's bug, and we removed it. Back any of the ten. But if you want the move with the smallest downside and the largest upside, the one that, done right, costs negative money because you are buying assets rather than burning cash, the author's own bet is the [Loving Takeover](../appendix/loving-takeover.qmd), and the [arithmetic of why it is asymmetric](../economics/investment-terms.qmd) is in the back. Not because it is the only door. Because it has the best math, and you were promised math.

## The actual cost

The cost is not money. It is the most expensive thing you own, which is your attention.

Right now you could be watching young ladies twerk on TikTok, which I am told is enormously fun and asks nothing of you. Or watching large groups of men elaborately relocate spheres from one location to another at great cost, an activity your species takes more seriously than most of its diseases. Or watching very rich people on television, who are stealing your money in elaborate ways, pay other people to make you furious at a different group who are stealing far less of it, in far less elaborate ways, while everyone faces the wrong direction.

Instead, someone is asking you to read a long (at least slightly hilarious?) book about how to avoid burning in hell forever in exchange for a possibly endless stretch of pleasantness.

In the short term this is the worse offer. In the long term it is the best trade ever made available to your species: a few evenings of not-twerking, weighed against infinity. The expected value is not close.

## Why this isn't Pascal's wager

Three centuries ago a Frenchman named Pascal noticed the same shape: a small bet for an infinite prize. His version is famous, and broken. This is the same machine with the broken parts replaced.

Here is the bet he drew, for anyone who has not seen it:

| You... | ...and God exists | ...and God does not |
|---|---|---|
| **Believe** | Infinite reward | You wasted some Sundays |
| **Don't believe** | Infinite punishment | You slept in |

Infinity beats Sundays, so he said believe. Here is the same shape with the bugs removed:

| You... | ...and the infinities are real | ...and they are not |
|---|---|---|
| **Act** (a share, an afternoon) | Your odds shift toward forever-flourishing and away from forever-suffering | You hold a real asset that does not go to zero and buy some healthy years. A gain on its own. |
| **Don't act** | You leave two infinities on the table | You keep the afternoon |

There is no losing box on the Act row. That is the whole repair. Pascal's bet had a cost cell (believe, then find there is no god, and the Sundays were for nothing); this one does not, because it is backed by assets and added years instead of faith. The four specific bugs:

| Pascal's wager breaks because | Love's Wager doesn't |
|---|---|
| You have to pick one god out of thousands, and might pick wrong | One diagnosis, about ten non-competing fixes. Back them all. Only one has to land. |
| There's no evidence for any of them | Medicine works. Lifespans went up. Experience is already adjustable. |
| Believing doesn't change the outcome | Funding trials demonstrably produces treatments. |
| The stake is your eternal soul | The stake is some evenings you were going to waste anyway. |

The "pick one god" problem is worse than picking wrong. Christianity alone runs about 47,000 separate denominations [@zurlo-christian-denominations-2024], never mind the thousands of other religions, and a great many of them promise damnation specifically for backing the wrong one. Pick a church at random and your odds of the correct one, if a correct one exists, are roughly 1 in 47,000, with a healthy share of the other 46,999 holding an eternity of punishment in reserve for whoever guessed wrong. So Pascal's bet was never a free lottery ticket. It was one that might detonate: choose the wrong god and you may be punished precisely for choosing, when sitting still would have cost you nothing. And since every one of those options dangles the same infinite prize, the arithmetic cannot tell you which to take. Infinity times one option is infinity; infinity times tens of thousands of mutually exclusive options is a number that points nowhere. Pascal's wager does not even resolve to an action. Love's Wager has no wrong door: the ten fixes do not compete, none of them damns you for backing another, and you may back all of them at once. And here is the part no theologian ever got: where nobody can compute which god is least wrong, you can. These mechanisms have probabilities and costs you can actually estimate, rank, and argue about, so even the "which one" question, the one that broke Pascal, is just arithmetic here. You do not go to hell for picking the wrong biotech god. You do the math, pick the least wrong one, and back the others too as insurance. You are not choosing one god out of thousands. You are funding a hospital, and the hospital does not care what you believe.

Pascal asked you to believe something you can't check, hoping to please something you can't detect. This asks you to read a book and do one of the ten things in it.

## If you won't believe in infinity

Fine. Delete the infinities.

Even the most boring, selfish version of these solutions pays off in plain dollars. Buy one share of a defense contractor and it's still an ordinary stock that doesn't go to zero. The campaign it funds still has a real, documented chance of paying off. And every extra healthy year any of this buys you keeps the rest of your money worth something, because [your money is worthless the day you die](../call-to-action/your-personal-benefits.qmd). The [finite math](../appendix/investor-risk-analysis.qmd) is already positive. The infinity was only ever the ceiling on top of a floor that already clears.

So the bet works on everyone. Believe in the infinities and you act because the payoff is unlimited. Refuse them and you act because the boring math says yes anyway. The only way to lose is to not play.

The interesting question was never whether the numbers work. It's whether knowing they work changes what you do next.

## The wager

The numbers came first. I offered you {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag_economic_value >}}, the price of the lives you are losing, and you would not trade one of your {{< var nuclear_winter_overkill_factor_nounit >}} apocalypses to take it. So the numbers were never going to do it. Hence infinity.

There is now an entity called Earth Optimization Services. It takes the proceeds from this manual, buys shares in the companies that build your missiles, and points their lobbyists the other way. This is the [Loving Takeover](../appendix/loving-takeover.qmd). The manual is free. The shares are the wager.

So the wager is yours now. Mine was a decade, on the chance you would read this. Yours is an afternoon, on the chance it is true.

## The useful hallucination

Every institution that runs your world is a fictional construct. Nations, corporations, money, laws, borders: none of them exist in physics. They exist because enough humans agreed to hallucinate them at the same time. Some of these shared hallucinations are very useful. Property rights, for instance, keep people from taking your things. Some of them are killing you. The one where you spend {{< var military_to_government_clinical_trials_spending_ratio >}} times more on the military than on curing your diseases is killing you.

Earth Optimization Services is just another collective hallucination. The only difference between it and the ones you already believe in is that this one, if enough of you agree to hallucinate it, buys the harmful hallucinations and turns them into helpful ones. The entire job is getting enough humans to hallucinate the right thing.

You have hallucinated worse.

## If you are busy

If you don't like war and/or disease, but you are very busy, but you have some money:

If you are **generous**, you can donate it at [warondisease.org/donate](https://warondisease.org/donate). It will be used to end war and/or disease.

If you are **greedy**, you can invest in Earth Optimization Services, LLC. The [investment terms](../economics/investment-terms.qmd) are designed so that ending war and disease makes you a great deal of money, because the companies we buy become more valuable when they stop making bombs and start making medicine. Greed and generosity arrive at the same destination. This was done on purpose.

## Welcome aboard

Congratulations. You are now a Humanity Manager at Earth Optimization Services. Your title is President of Earth Optimization Services, and the correct way to address you is Your Excellency. You are entitled to a vote in how it is run, and to a better world every time it succeeds. You cannot buy that vote and you cannot sell it; it is yours because you live here. As a Humanity Manager, we would appreciate it if you would be nice and helpful to the other humans in the workplace, which is Earth.

Thank you.
